The eruption produced enormous amounts of carbon dioxide, which enhanced the greenhouse effect and disrupted normal weather patterns, causing widespread storm activity that blocked sunlight.
The eruption released water vapor into the atmosphere that formed a global cloud layer, reflecting sunlight back into space and reducing surface temperatures for more than a year.
The eruption produced so much ash that the global atmosphere was permanently darkened, reducing photosynthesis in crops across the entire Northern Hemisphere for decades.

questions.text: James Hutton proposed uniformitarianism in the late 1700s. Which of the following best describes what uniformitarianism claims?

answers.text: Earth is approximately 6,000 years old, and its geological features were formed rapidly by a series of catastrophic floods.
Geological features form at unpredictable rates that vary by location, making it impossible to compare rock layers from different regions.

The geological processes acting on Earth today (erosion, deposition, volcanic activity) are the same kinds of processes that shaped Earth in the past, and they have operated over an immense span of time.
Earth's geological history is divided into separate intervals defined by sudden, dramatic changes that are fundamentally different from any process operating today.

questions.text: A geologist examining a cliff face sees three horizontal sedimentary rock layers (oldest at the bottom, youngest at the top) cut through by a diagonal vein of granite. Using the principle of cross-cutting relationships, what can she conclude about the granite?

answers.text: The granite formed after the top layer only, because the cross-cutting relationship applies only to the youngest layer the intrusion contacts.
The granite formed at the same time as the middle sedimentary layer, because it is found in contact with all three layers.
The granite formed after all three sedimentary layers, because an intrusion can only cut through rock that already exists.
The granite formed before the sedimentary layers, because granite is a harder rock and must have formed first.

questions.text: A mold fossil and a cast fossil often occur together. Which of the following correctly distinguishes them?

answers.text: A mold fossil is the impression (negative space) left when an organism dissolves or decays in sediment; a cast fossil forms when minerals fill that impression and harden, producing a three-dimensional replica of the original.
A mold fossil is three-dimensional; a cast fossil is a two-dimensional impression on a rock surface.
A mold fossil preserves soft tissue; a cast fossil preserves only hard parts such as shells and bones.
A mold fossil is created when organic material is replaced atom-by-atom with minerals (permineralization); a cast fossil is the original hard parts preserved in sediment.

questions.text: A geologist is searching for an index fossil to correlate rock layers across two different continents. Which combination of characteristics would make an organism the best candidate for an index fossil?

answers.text: Long-lived species with a wide geographic range, because its presence across many locations confirms its reliability as a marker.
Long-lived species with a small geographic range and hard shells that preserve well in sediment.
Short-lived species (existed for a brief geological interval) that was geographically widespread and abundant, leaving distinctive, easily identified remains.
Short-lived species confined to deep-water marine environments, because deep-water sediments are better preserved and less disturbed by erosion.

questions.text: Approximately what percentage of Earth's total history is represented by the Phanerozoic eon, which spans from the Cambrian explosion (~541 Ma) to the present?

answers.text: About 50 percent -- roughly half of Earth's 4.54-billion-year history.
About 88 percent -- the Phanerozoic eon is the longest of Earth's eons.
About 12 percent -- the entire history of complex animal life represents only a small fraction of Earth's age.
About 30 percent -- roughly the time since the first eukaryotes evolved.

questions.text: What defines the boundaries between intervals (eons, eras, periods) on the geologic time scale?

answers.text: Geographic boundaries -- each interval is defined by the position of the continents at that time in Earth's history.
Changes in rock type -- each new interval begins when the dominant rock type changes from sedimentary to igneous or vice versa.
Equal divisions of elapsed time -- each interval represents the same number of millions of years.
Major transitions in the fossil record, most commonly mass extinctions followed by the rapid diversification of new life forms in the subsequent layers.

questions.text: The Great Oxidation Event (~2.4 billion years ago) caused what has been described as the first mass extinction in Earth's history. Which of the following best explains why?

answers.text: The increase in atmospheric oxygen destroyed the ozone layer, exposing surface organisms to harmful ultraviolet radiation that caused mass die-offs.
The rapid accumulation of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere was toxic to the anaerobic organisms that then dominated life, because their metabolic systems had no way to handle or use free oxygen.
The oxygen produced by cyanobacteria combined with iron in the oceans to form iron oxide, which sank to the seafloor and removed the iron that marine organisms needed to survive.
The Great Oxidation Event raised global temperatures by intensifying the greenhouse effect, causing a period of extreme warming that eliminated most of the organisms alive at the time.

questions.text: Which Milankovitch cycle operates on the longest timescale and is most closely associated with the dominant ~100,000-year rhythm observed in glacial-interglacial cycles of the past 800,000 years?

answers.text: Eccentricity, the change in the shape of Earth's orbit from nearly circular to slightly more elliptical, which cycles over approximately 100,000 years.
Precession, the wobble of Earth's rotational axis, which completes a full cycle in approximately 26,000 years.
Insolation, the total variation in solar energy output, which fluctuates on an 11-year solar cycle that compounds over geological time.
Obliquity, the change in Earth's axial tilt, which cycles between approximately 22.1 and 24.5 degrees over ~41,000 years.

questions.text: Ice cores drilled from the Antarctic ice sheet preserve a climate record extending back approximately 800,000 years. What physical mechanism allows the ice to preserve ancient atmospheric chemistry?

answers.text: Annual snowfall accumulates in layers that compress into ice; as snow compresses, tiny air bubbles are trapped within the ice, preserving samples of the atmosphere at the time the snow fell.
Isotopic fractionation during freezing causes greenhouse gases to concentrate in the lower layers of an ice sheet, where they can be extracted and dated.
Volcanic ash layers deposited on the ice surface form a chemical seal that prevents atmospheric gases from escaping the ice over geological time.
Ice at depth undergoes recrystallization that chemically bonds atmospheric gases into the crystal structure, preserving them until the ice is melted for analysis.

questions.text: The 800,000-year Antarctic ice core record shows that atmospheric CO2 concentrations during the warmest interglacial periods peaked at approximately 280-300 ppm. In recent years, measured CO2 at Mauna Loa Observatory has exceeded 420 ppm. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this comparison?

answers.text: Current CO2 concentrations are unprecedented in Earth's entire geological history, meaning CO2 has never been this high at any point since Earth formed 4.54 billion years ago.
The current CO2 level is only 40 percent higher than the natural interglacial maximum and therefore represents a modest change unlikely to have significant climate consequences.
The comparison proves that human industrial activity is the sole cause of the current CO2 increase, because the ice core record eliminates all other possible explanations.

Current CO2 levels are higher than at any point in the 800,000-year ice core record, indicating that the atmosphere is in a state outside the range of natural glacial-interglacial variation documented by that record.

questions.text: Aristotle claimed that heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones. Galileo's inclined plane experiments showed this was incorrect. Which of the following best states Galileo's conclusion?

answers.text: All objects fall at the same rate in the absence of air resistance, because gravitational acceleration is independent of an object's mass.
Objects only fall at the same rate when they are made of the same material -- Galileo found that material composition determines fall speed.
Heavier objects do fall faster, but only slightly -- Galileo refined Aristotle's values rather than overturning them.
All objects fall at different rates depending on their shape, not their mass -- a sphere always falls faster than a cube of the same weight.

questions.text: A spacecraft traveling at 15,000 m/s in deep space turns off its engines. There is no air resistance and no significant gravitational pull from any nearby body. What does Newton's First Law predict will happen to the spacecraft's velocity?

answers.text: It gradually slows to a stop over several hours, because motion naturally decreases without an engine to maintain it.
It slows momentarily, then returns to 15,000 m/s, because the spacecraft seeks its "natural" equilibrium speed.
It continues at 15,000 m/s in a straight line indefinitely, because the net force on it is zero.
It speeds up, because removing the engine's backward exhaust thrust allows the spacecraft to accelerate freely.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly defines inertia?

answers.text: The friction force that opposes the motion of an object sliding across a surface.
The energy stored in a moving object due to its velocity.
The force of gravity acting on an object's mass.
The tendency of an object to resist any change in its state of motion -- whether at rest or moving.

questions.text: A net force of 15 N acts on a 3 kg object. What is the object's acceleration?

answers.text: 0.2 m/s², because acceleration equals mass divided by force.
5 m/s², because a = F/m = 15 N / 3 kg = 5 m/s².
12 m/s², because acceleration equals force minus mass.
45 m/s², because acceleration equals force multiplied by mass.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly states what the SI unit Newton (N) equals in terms of base SI units?

answers.text: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s² (kilogram-meters per second squared)
1 N = 1 kg/m/s (kilograms per meter per second)
1 N = 1 kg·m/s (kilogram-meters per second)
1 N = 1 kg/m/s² (kilograms per meter per second squared)

questions.text: A 50 kg student stands on a scale on the surface of the Moon, where the gravitational acceleration is approximately 1.63 m/s². What is the student's mass on the Moon, and what is their weight on the Moon?

answers.text: Mass = 50 kg; weight = 490 N (same as on Earth, because weight is a constant property).
Mass = 50 kg; weight = 0 N (astronauts are weightless on the Moon).
Mass = 50 kg; weight = 81.5 N.
Mass = 8.1 kg (reduced because the Moon's gravity is weaker); weight = 81.5 N.

questions.text: Newton's Third Law states that for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. A student argues that this means all forces in the universe cancel out and nothing can ever accelerate. What is wrong with this reasoning?

answers.text: The student is wrong because action and reaction forces act on different objects and therefore cannot cancel each other. Forces cancel only when they act on the same object.
The student is wrong because the Third Law only applies to contact forces, not to gravity or other field forces.
The student is wrong because action and reaction forces are not always exactly equal -- they are only approximately equal for small objects.
The student is correct; Newton's Third Law does mean all forces cancel, but objects can still accelerate because of velocity already stored in them.

questions.text: A book rests on a table. Earth pulls the book downward with a gravitational force of 20 N. According to Newton's Third Law, what is the reaction to this gravitational force?

answers.text: The table pushes the book upward with a normal force of 20 N.
Gravity pulls the table downward with a force of 20 N.
The book pushes down on the table with a contact force of 20 N.
The book pulls Earth upward with a gravitational force of 20 N.

questions.text: A net force of 10 N is applied to a 2 kg object, giving it an acceleration of 5 m/s². If the mass is doubled to 4 kg while the same 10 N force is applied, what is the new acceleration?

answers.text: 5 m/s², because acceleration depends only on force, not on mass.
20 m/s², because a heavier object stores more energy and therefore accelerates faster under the same force.
2.5 m/s², because doubling the mass while keeping the force constant halves the acceleration.
10 m/s², because doubling the mass doubles the acceleration when force stays the same.

questions.text: Which of the following is the best example of Newton's Third Law in action?

answers.text: A ball thrown upward slows down as it rises because gravity exerts a constant downward force, reducing the ball's upward velocity.
A rocket accelerates upward in space because it expels hot gas downward, and the expelled gas exerts an equal and opposite force pushing the rocket upward.
A skydiver reaches terminal velocity because air resistance equals the gravitational force -- the two forces on the skydiver balance to zero net force.
A book rests on a table in equilibrium because the table's normal force exactly equals the gravitational force on the book.

questions.text: According to Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation, if the distance between two objects is doubled while their masses remain the same, the gravitational force between them becomes:

answers.text: Twice as large, because force is proportional to distance.
Unchanged, because the masses have not changed.
One-quarter as large, because force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
One-half as large, because force is inversely proportional to the distance.

questions.text: In Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation (F = Gm₁m₂/r²), the symbol G represents:

answers.text: The universal gravitational constant, approximately 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², which relates mass and distance to gravitational force for any two objects anywhere in the universe.
The gravitational acceleration of any freely falling object, equal to the object's weight divided by its mass.
The local gravitational field strength on Earth's surface (9.8 m/s²), which varies from planet to planet.
The orbital speed of a satellite, which depends on the planet's mass and the satellite's orbital radius.

questions.text: A 60 kg astronaut on Earth weighs approximately 588 N. The same astronaut travels to a planet where the gravitational field strength is 3.7 m/s². Which statement is correct about the astronaut's mass and weight on that planet?

answers.text: The weight remains 588 N, but the mass decreases, because mass is determined by the gravitational field and would be lower in a weaker field.
The mass remains 60 kg, but the weight decreases to 60 × 3.7 = 222 N, because weight depends on the local gravitational field strength.
Both the mass and the weight remain 60 kg and 588 N, because the astronaut's body has not changed.
Both the mass and the weight decrease proportionally, because a weaker gravitational field reduces the amount of matter an object contains in that environment.

questions.text: A book rests on a horizontal table. Which of the following correctly describes the direction of the normal force the table exerts on the book?

answers.text: Horizontally, parallel to the table surface, because contact forces act along the surface.
Perpendicular to the table surface, pointing upward away from the table, opposing the book's weight.
Straight down, in the same direction as the book's weight, because both forces are gravity-related and act toward Earth's center.
At an angle between the surface and vertical, splitting the difference between weight and any horizontal forces acting on the book.

questions.text: A heavy crate sits on a warehouse floor. A worker pushes on the crate with 200 N but it does not move. The coefficient of static friction between the crate and the floor is 0.45 and the crate's weight is 980 N. Which statement best describes the friction force on the crate?

answers.text: Static friction equals 441 N (= 0.45 × 980 N) because the friction force always equals the coefficient times the normal force, regardless of the applied force.
Static friction equals 980 N, equal to the weight of the crate, because the floor must support both the weight and resist any horizontal force.
Static friction equals zero because the crate is not moving.
Static friction equals 200 N, because when an object is stationary and the applied force is below the maximum, static friction adjusts to exactly balance the applied force.

questions.text: An object moves at constant speed in a circle. In which direction does its centripetal acceleration point?

answers.text: In the same direction as the object's velocity, tangent to the circular path.
Toward the center of the circle, perpendicular to the velocity at every point.
Away from the center of the circle, in the direction of the apparent centrifugal force.
Straight down, because gravity provides the centripetal acceleration in all circular motion.

questions.text: A car rounds a flat, horizontal, circular curve. What provides the centripetal force that keeps the car on its curved path?

answers.text: The centrifugal reaction force from the car's inertia, which balances the car's tendency to go straight.
Gravity, which pulls the car toward Earth's center and also inward toward the center of the curve.
Static friction between the tires and the road surface, acting sideways toward the inside of the curve.
The engine force, which pushes the car forward and can be redirected inward during a turn.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly states Kepler's First Law of planetary motion?

answers.text: The orbits of the planets are perfect circles, with the Sun at the center of each circular orbit.
The square of each planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its average orbital radius.
The orbits of the planets are ellipses, with the Sun located at one focus of each ellipse.
A line connecting each planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals as the planet moves.

questions.text: Kepler's Second Law states that a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals. Which of the following correctly describes what this means for a planet's orbital speed?

answers.text: The planet moves at constant speed throughout its orbit, because equal areas in equal times requires uniform motion.
The planet moves at the same average speed regardless of its distance from the Sun, since the total area swept per year is fixed.
The planet moves faster when farther from the Sun and slower when closer, to compensate for the larger orbital radius.
The planet moves faster when closer to the Sun (near perihelion) and slower when farther from the Sun (near aphelion).

questions.text: A satellite in circular orbit around Earth is described as being "in free fall." Which explanation best captures what this means?

answers.text: The satellite is slowing down gradually due to gravity, and "free fall" refers to the fact that it will eventually fall to Earth when it slows down enough.

The satellite is continuously falling toward Earth due to gravity, but its horizontal speed is high enough that the curved Earth surface falls away beneath it at the same rate, so it continuously misses the surface.
The satellite moves in a straight line at constant speed because the centrifugal force exactly cancels Earth's gravity, resulting in zero net force.
The satellite experiences zero gravity because it is far enough from Earth that Earth's gravitational field does not reach it.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly states the formula for work done by a force, and identifies what the angle in the formula represents?

answers.text: W = F / d · cosθ, where θ is the angle between the applied force and gravity; larger angles mean less work.
W = F · d · cosθ, where θ is the angle between the direction of the force and the direction of displacement; only the component of force in the direction of motion does work.
W = F · d · sinθ, where θ is the angle between the force vector and the direction of displacement; the sine component represents the direction of motion.
W = F · d, where force and displacement are always measured in the same direction, so no angle factor is needed.

questions.text: A person carries a briefcase horizontally at constant height from one end of a hallway to the other. Which of the following correctly describes the work done by gravity on the briefcase during this trip?

answers.text: Gravity does positive work equal to mgh, where h is the height the briefcase is carried above the floor.
Gravity does negative work equal to −mgd, where d is the horizontal distance traveled, because gravity opposes the horizontal motion.
Gravity does zero work on the briefcase because the gravitational force acts downward while the displacement is horizontal; the angle between force and displacement is 90 degrees, making cos 90° = 0.
Gravity does work equal to mgd because gravity is always acting on the briefcase and the briefcase moves a distance d.

questions.text: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object equals:

answers.text: the change in the object's kinetic energy: W<sub>net</sub> = KE<sub>final</sub> − KE<sub>initial</sub>.
the product of the object's mass and its final velocity: W<sub>net</sub> = mv<sub>final</sub>.
the total potential energy stored in the object at the end of the motion.
the object's weight multiplied by the total distance it traveled.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly states the formula for kinetic energy and identifies the units?

answers.text: KE = ½mv², measured in Joules.
KE = mv², measured in Newtons.
KE = ½mv, measured in Joules.
KE = 2mv, measured in kilogram-meters per second.

questions.text: A car increases its speed from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. By what factor does its kinetic energy increase?

answers.text: The kinetic energy increases by a factor of 2, because doubling the speed doubles the kinetic energy.
The kinetic energy increases by a factor of 8, because kinetic energy depends on v³ for high-speed objects.
The kinetic energy increases by a factor of 1, because kinetic energy depends on mass and the mass does not change.
The kinetic energy increases by a factor of 4, because kinetic energy depends on v² and (20)²/(10)² = 400/100 = 4.

questions.text: The law of conservation of energy states that:

answers.text: energy can be created by chemical reactions but cannot be destroyed; the total amount of energy in the universe is increasing.
the total energy of a closed system remains constant; energy is never created from nothing and never destroyed, only transformed from one form to another.
kinetic energy and potential energy are always equal to each other in any mechanical system.
mechanical energy (KE + PE) is conserved in all systems, including those with friction.

questions.text: A frictionless pendulum is released from rest at a height h above its lowest point. At the lowest point of its swing, which statement correctly describes the energy state of the pendulum?

answers.text: All of the pendulum's initial gravitational potential energy has converted to kinetic energy; KE at the bottom equals mgh.
The kinetic energy at the bottom is equal to half the initial potential energy; the other half has been lost to the environment.
The pendulum has zero total mechanical energy because it started from rest, and rest implies no energy.
The pendulum's kinetic energy at the bottom equals its potential energy at the top minus its weight times the height.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly states the formula for power and the SI unit in which it is measured?

answers.text: P = m · v / t, measured in Newtons (N), where power is the rate of change of momentum.
P = F · d, measured in Joules (J), where power is the total work done over a given distance.
P = W/t, measured in Watts (W), where 1 Watt = 1 Joule per second.
P = W · t, measured in Watt-seconds (Ws), where power is the product of work and time elapsed.

questions.text: A lever has an effort arm of 3 m and a load arm of 0.5 m. A 100 N force is applied at the effort end. What does the lever accomplish, and what does it not accomplish?

answers.text: The lever creates energy: the mechanical advantage of 6 means the output force is 6 times the input, so output energy exceeds input energy by a factor of 6.
The lever amplifies the total work output: 600 N of load force over 3 m equals 1,800 J, which is greater than the 300 J of input work.
The lever reduces the total work required: by multiplying force, it allows the same task to be completed with less total energy expended.
The lever multiplies the force (IMA = 6, so it produces 600 N from 100 N input) but does not change the total energy: the output force acts over a shorter distance, keeping work in equal to work out.

questions.text: A machine has an input energy of 500 J and produces 350 J of useful work output. What is its efficiency, and what happens to the remaining energy?

answers.text: Efficiency = 70%; the remaining 150 J is converted to thermal energy (heat) through friction and other non-conservative forces, warming the machine and its surroundings.
Efficiency = 150%; the machine adds 150 J more than it uses because friction helps rather than hinders energy output.
Efficiency = 70%; the remaining 30% is stored as potential energy inside the machine, available for future use.
Efficiency = 70%; the remaining 150 J is destroyed by friction and no longer exists as energy.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes what heat is?

answers.text: A substance stored in warm objects and released when they cool down, originally described as "caloric."
The average kinetic energy per particle in a substance, measured on the Kelvin scale.
The total kinetic energy of all particles in an object, which increases when the object is warmed.
The transfer of thermal energy from a warmer object to a cooler one due to a temperature difference.

questions.text: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been sitting at room temperature (22°C) for several hours. When you pick up each one, the metal spoon feels noticeably colder. What is the correct explanation?

answers.text: The metal spoon has a lower temperature because its shiny surface reflects heat and prevents it from warming fully.
Both spoons are at 22°C, but wood contains more stored thermal energy per gram, so it transfers more heat to your hand and feels warmer.
Both spoons are at 22°C, but the metal conducts heat away from your hand much faster than wood, causing your hand to lose heat rapidly and creating the sensation of cold.
The metal spoon has a lower temperature than the wooden spoon because metal absorbs more cold from the room air.

questions.text: Which of the following is the best statement of the First Law of Thermodynamics?

answers.text: The entropy of an isolated system always increases or remains constant; it never spontaneously decreases.
The total energy of an isolated system is conserved: the change in internal energy equals the heat added minus the work done by the system (ΔU = Q − W).
It is impossible to reduce the temperature of any system to absolute zero in a finite number of steps.
No heat engine can convert all the heat it receives from a hot reservoir into useful mechanical work.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly states what the Second Law of Thermodynamics says about the entropy of an isolated system?

answers.text: Entropy may increase or decrease depending on whether the process is exothermic or endothermic.
Entropy decreases as the system reaches thermal equilibrium.
Entropy always increases or remains constant; it never spontaneously decreases in an isolated system.
Entropy remains exactly constant in all real physical processes.

questions.text: A heat engine operates between a hot reservoir at 500 K and a cold reservoir at 250 K. Using the Carnot efficiency formula, what is the maximum possible efficiency of this engine?

answers.text: 25%, because real engines always achieve one-half the Carnot limit, and the theoretical Carnot efficiency here is 50%.
100%, because the temperature ratio Tₕ/Tᴄ = 500/250 = 2.0, and the engine can theoretically convert twice the cold reservoir temperature into work.
50%, calculated as 1 − Tᴄ/Tₕ = 1 − 250/500 = 0.50.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes what happens during nuclear fission?

answers.text: Two light nuclei (such as hydrogen isotopes) are forced together to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy because the product has less mass than the reactants.
A nucleus emits an alpha or beta particle, reducing its atomic number by one or two units and releasing a small amount of energy in the process.
Chemical bonds between atoms are broken and reformed, releasing energy stored in the electromagnetic attraction between electrons and nuclei.
A heavy nucleus (such as uranium-235) absorbs a neutron, becomes unstable, and splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing additional neutrons and energy.

questions.text: In the equation E = mc², what does the variable m represent, and why does a small value of m correspond to an enormous value of E?

answers.text: m is the total mass of the fuel before the reaction; all of this mass is converted to energy, which is why nuclear reactions are powerful.
m is the temperature in Kelvin; the equation converts temperature to equivalent energy, which is why hotter reactions release more energy.

m is the mass deficit: the small difference between the mass of the reactants and the mass of the products, which is converted to energy. Because c² = 9 × 10<sup>16</sup> m²/s² is an enormous number, even a tiny mass deficit produces an enormous energy release.
m is the momentum of the particles involved in the reaction; momentum is converted to energy in nuclear reactions at relativistic speeds.

questions.text: Water has a specific heat of 4.18 J/g°C and aluminum has a specific heat of 0.90 J/g°C. The same amount of heat is added to 100 g of water and to 100 g of aluminum. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: Neither changes temperature, because heat only changes the state of a substance.
The aluminum warms up more, because less heat is needed to raise the temperature of each gram of aluminum by one degree.
The water warms up more, because water has the higher specific heat.
Both warm up by the same amount, because they receive the same amount of heat.

questions.text: Solar and wind power are the cheapest sources of new electricity generation in most of the world, yet grid operators still rely on other energy sources to meet demand. Which of the following best explains why?

answers.text: Solar panels and wind turbines have shorter lifespans than fossil fuel plants and must be replaced so frequently that their total cost exceeds the cost of conventional generation.

Solar and wind are intermittent: they generate electricity only when the sun shines and wind blows, so the grid needs storage or backup generation to maintain reliable supply when they are unavailable.
Solar and wind cannot be integrated with the existing grid infrastructure because they produce direct current (DC) electricity that is incompatible with the alternating current (AC) grid.
Solar and wind energy are too diffuse to be collected efficiently; the land area required makes them impractical for large-scale electricity generation.

questions.text: A pot of water at 100°C is boiling on a stove, and heat continues to flow into the water. Why does the temperature of the water stay at 100°C while it boils?

answers.text: Water cannot absorb any more heat energy once it reaches 100°C.
The stove stops transferring heat once the water reaches 100°C.
The water molecules stop moving once the water reaches its boiling point.
The added heat is going into changing the water from liquid to gas by overcoming attractions between molecules, rather than raising the temperature.

questions.text: A student observes ripples on a pond after dropping a stone in the water. A cork floating on the surface bobs up and down as each ripple passes but does not drift toward the shore. Which of the following best describes what this observation demonstrates about waves?

answers.text: The frequency of the wave equals the speed at which the cork moves up and down.
The energy of the wave is stored in the cork, which is why the cork does not move sideways.
Waves are disturbances that transfer energy through a medium without permanently displacing the matter of that medium.
Waves can only travel on the surface of liquids; they cannot travel through solids or gases.

questions.text: A sound wave in air has a frequency of 256 Hz and a wavelength of 1.34 m. What is the wave speed?

answers.text: 257 m/s. Add frequency and wavelength: 256 + 1.34 ≈ 257.

questions.text: An astronaut in orbit outside the International Space Station drops a tool. It makes no sound that the astronaut can hear, even though it strikes the station's exterior. Which of the following correctly explains this?

answers.text: The tool does not vibrate when it strikes the station in a vacuum.
Sound waves lose all their energy over short distances in a vacuum.
Sound in space travels at a different speed than on Earth, making it inaudible to the human ear.
Sound is a mechanical wave that requires a medium of molecules to propagate; the near-vacuum of space contains essentially no molecules, so no pressure wave can form or travel.

questions.text: A train moving toward a stationary observer sounds its horn. Compared to the actual frequency the horn emits, what frequency does the observer hear?

answers.text: A lower frequency, because the train is moving away from the horn's sound waves, stretching them out.
A higher frequency, because the train's motion compresses the wavefronts ahead of it, shortening the wavelength and increasing the frequency detected by the observer.
The same frequency, because the speed of sound in air is independent of the speed of the source.
A lower frequency, because the horn's sound energy must overcome the distance the train is traveling.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly orders the main regions of the electromagnetic spectrum from lowest energy per photon to highest energy per photon?

answers.text: Visible light, infrared, radio, microwave, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray.
Radio, infrared, X-ray, microwave, visible light, ultraviolet, gamma ray.
Gamma ray, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwave, radio.
Radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about the speed of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum is correct?

answers.text: Gamma rays travel faster than radio waves in vacuum because they carry more energy.
The speed of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum depends on its frequency; higher-frequency waves travel faster.
Radio waves travel faster than visible light in vacuum because their longer wavelength allows them to cover more distance per cycle.
All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum (c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s), regardless of frequency or wavelength.

questions.text: A beam of light strikes a flat mirror. The angle between the incoming beam and the mirror's surface is 35 degrees. What is the angle of reflection, measured from the normal?

answers.text: 35 degrees from the mirror surface, which is the same as 35 degrees from the normal.
70 degrees from the normal.
55 degrees from the normal.
35 degrees from the normal.

questions.text: A ray of light passes from air into a glass block at an angle. What happens to the light at the air-glass boundary?

answers.text: The light slows down and, if it enters at any angle other than perpendicular, bends away from the normal.
The light speeds up, because the denser glass provides more material for the light to push against.
The light continues in the same direction but slows down, because glass absorbs some of its energy.
The light slows down and, if it enters at any angle other than perpendicular, bends toward the normal, because glass has a higher index of refraction than air.

questions.text: A scientist heats a sample of pure sodium gas and observes the light it emits through a diffraction grating. She sees two bright yellow lines on an otherwise dark background at specific wavelengths. What do these bright yellow lines represent?

answers.text: All the wavelengths of visible light that sodium reflects; the dark regions are the wavelengths it absorbs.

The unique emission spectrum of sodium: specific wavelengths of light produced when electrons in sodium atoms fall from higher energy levels to lower ones, releasing photons of those exact frequencies.
The emission spectrum of the heating element, which always produces yellow light at high temperatures.
Background radiation from the Sun that sodium atoms scatter in the yellow portion of the spectrum.

questions.text: The spectrum of sunlight shows hundreds of dark lines crossing an otherwise continuous rainbow. Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen showed in 1859 that these dark lines correspond exactly to the emission lines of known elements. What is the correct explanation for the dark lines in the solar spectrum?

answers.text: The dark lines are gaps in the solar spectrum produced when the Sun's nuclear reactions consume specific wavelengths of radiation as fuel.
The dark lines are an artifact of passing sunlight through Earth's atmosphere, which adds dark lines at wavelengths corresponding to nitrogen and oxygen absorption.
Elements in the Sun's cooler outer atmosphere absorb specific wavelengths from the continuous spectrum produced by the hotter interior, leaving dark gaps at exactly those wavelengths.
The dark lines are caused by interstellar dust between Earth and the Sun, which absorbs light at specific wavelengths before it reaches Earth.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes a light-year?

answers.text: The distance light travels in one year, approximately 9.46 trillion kilometers
The time it takes light to travel from the Sun to Earth
The time required for the Sun to complete one orbit of the Milky Way
The average distance between Earth and the Sun

questions.text: What does one astronomical unit (AU) represent?

answers.text: The distance from Earth to the nearest star, Proxima Centauri
The distance light travels in one second
The average distance between Earth and the Sun, approximately 150 million kilometers
The diameter of the Milky Way galaxy

questions.text: Astronomers use the "cosmic distance ladder" because

answers.text: The parallax method can measure distances to any star in the observable universe
No single measurement technique is accurate enough to work at all cosmic scales
Standard candles like Cepheid variables only work within the Milky Way
Redshift is the only reliable method for measuring distances beyond the solar system

questions.text: On a standard H-R diagram, where are white dwarf stars located?

answers.text: Upper right: high luminosity, cool temperature
Upper left: high luminosity, hot temperature

Along the diagonal main sequence, near the middle

G

questions.text: The visible surface of the Sun from which light escapes into space is called the

answers.text: Photosphere

questions.text: In the proton-proton chain, what are the starting material and the end product?

answers.text: Helium nuclei fusing into carbon; energy released as gamma rays
Electrons and protons fusing into neutrons; energy released as neutrinos
Hydrogen nuclei (protons) fusing into helium nuclei; energy released in the process

questions.text: What determines whether a massive star's supernova remnant becomes a neutron star or a black hole?

answers.text: The temperature of the star at the moment of core collapse
The mass of the remnant core after the explosion
The age of the star when it explodes
Whether the star was part of a binary system

questions.text: Henrietta Swan Leavitt's discovery of the period-luminosity relationship in Cepheid variable stars was important because it

answers.text: Made it possible to determine the intrinsic brightness of a star from its pulsation period, enabling reliable distance measurements
Showed that all variable stars eventually become supernovae
Provided the first direct evidence that the universe is expanding
Proved that the Milky Way is the only galaxy in the universe

questions.text: The observable universe has a radius of approximately 46 billion light-years even though the universe is only about 13.8 billion years old. The best explanation for this is

answers.text: Astronomers have made a measurement error and the universe must be older than 13.8 billion years
Light travels faster than the speed of light in some regions of space
The universe was much smaller when the oldest light was emitted, and it has expanded during the time that light has been traveling toward us
The speed of light was different in the early universe

questions.text: According to the nebular hypothesis, why did the collapsing gas cloud that formed our solar system flatten into a disk rather than collapsing into a sphere?

answers.text: The Sun's gravity pulled material outward from the poles more strongly than from the equator
The conservation of angular momentum caused the rotating cloud to spin faster and flatten as it collapsed
The cloud was originally disk-shaped before it began collapsing
Radiation pressure from the proto-Sun pushed gas and dust away from the center

questions.text: What physical condition defines the frost line in the early solar system, and what does it determine?

answers.text: The temperature boundary beyond which volatile compounds like water and methane can freeze into solid form
The distance at which the Sun's magnetic field can no longer deflect solar wind particles
The zone where rocky material transitions to metallic material under increasing pressure
The point at which the Sun's gravity is too weak to hold smaller bodies in orbit

questions.text: The late heavy bombardment is one of the most significant events in early Earth's history. Which of the following best describes the primary evidence scientists use to identify it?

answers.text: Chemical signatures in Earth's oldest sedimentary rocks showing elevated iridium levels
The ages of lunar craters and rock samples returned by Apollo missions, which cluster between 3.8 and 4.1 billion years old
Ancient volcanic rock formations on Earth dated to approximately 4 billion years ago
Computer models of planetary orbital resonances that predict an impact surge

questions.text: Venus is actually hotter than Mercury despite being approximately twice as far from the Sun. What is the primary reason for this?

answers.text: Venus has a higher concentration of radioactive elements in its interior that heat the surface
Venus rotates so slowly that its sunlit side accumulates heat continuously for months at a time
Venus's dense carbon dioxide atmosphere traps outgoing infrared radiation, creating an extreme greenhouse effect
Venus is closer to the Sun than Earth, so it receives enough additional solar energy to be hotter

questions.text: Mars shows extensive evidence of a wetter past. Which of the following is NOT a type of evidence used to support this conclusion?

answers.text: A thick carbon dioxide atmosphere similar to Earth's that indicates past rainfall
Sedimentary rock layers deposited in ancient lake beds, identified by Mars rovers
Ancient riverbeds and delta formations visible from orbit
Minerals such as phyllosilicates that form only in the presence of liquid water

questions.text: Jupiter's moon Europa is considered one of the most promising candidates for life in the solar system even though it is far beyond the traditional habitable zone. What energy source keeps its subsurface ocean liquid?

answers.text: Chemical reactions between Europa's ice and Jupiter's magnetic field generate sufficient heat
Reflected sunlight from Jupiter's cloud bands warms Europa's surface enough to melt interior ice
Tidal heating caused by gravitational flexing from Jupiter's enormous gravity keeps Europa's interior warm
Radioactive decay in Europa's rocky interior provides enough heat to prevent freezing

questions.text: What is the key compositional difference that separates "gas giants" (Jupiter and Saturn) from "ice giants" (Uranus and Neptune)?

answers.text: Gas giants are entirely gaseous with no solid core, while ice giants have a completely solid frozen interior
Gas giants are composed primarily of hydrogen and helium, while ice giants have interiors dominated by hot, dense fluid water, methane, and ammonia
Gas giants formed inside the frost line while ice giants formed outside it, explaining the difference in their compositions
Gas giants have ring systems made of gas particles while ice giant ring systems are made of solid ice

questions.text: Saturn's moon Titan and Enceladus are both considered potentially habitable environments. Which pairing correctly matches each moon with its most notable habitability-relevant feature?

answers.text: Titan: subsurface liquid water ocean confirmed by geysers; Enceladus: thick nitrogen atmosphere with liquid methane lakes
Titan: confirmed presence of organic molecules raining from the sky onto an ice surface; Enceladus: rocky seafloor exposed directly to space
Titan: thick nitrogen atmosphere with surface liquid methane lakes; Enceladus: subsurface liquid water ocean evidenced by active water vapor geysers
Titan: active volcanoes heated by Saturn's tidal forces; Enceladus: dense atmosphere protecting surface from radiation

questions.text: The Kuiper Belt and the Oort Cloud are both reservoirs of small icy bodies in the outer solar system. What is the key structural difference between them?

answers.text: The Kuiper Belt is a disk-shaped region near the plane of the solar system, while the Oort Cloud is a theoretical spherical shell surrounding the entire solar system at much greater distance
The Kuiper Belt contains only rocky asteroids, while the Oort Cloud contains only icy comets
The Kuiper Belt is located between Mars and Jupiter, while the Oort Cloud is located beyond Neptune
The Kuiper Belt has been directly observed by spacecraft, while the Oort Cloud's existence has been confirmed by infrared telescope surveys

questions.text: In 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet. Which criterion did Pluto fail to meet under the new definition?

answers.text: Pluto does not orbit the Sun on a stable path; its orbit crosses Neptune's at certain points
Pluto is too small to be considered a planet under the new minimum mass requirement
Pluto has not cleared the neighborhood around its orbit; it shares its orbital region with many other Kuiper Belt objects
Pluto is not roughly spherical; its irregular shape disqualifies it from planetary status

questions.text: Which of the following best describes what Hubble's Law states?

answers.text: The speed at which a galaxy recedes from us is proportional to its distance from us
The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old, based on the rate of expansion
The redshift of a galaxy's light is caused by the galaxy spinning rapidly on its axis
Distant galaxies are older than nearby galaxies and therefore dimmer

questions.text: What physical phenomenon causes the redshift observed in the light from distant galaxies?

answers.text: The stretching of light waves as space itself expands between the galaxy and the observer
Distant galaxies contain older, cooler stars that emit redder light by nature
Absorption of blue light by intergalactic dust between galaxies and Earth
The Doppler effect caused by galaxies physically moving away at high speed through static space

questions.text: Henrietta Leavitt's discovery of the period-luminosity relationship in Cepheid variable stars was important primarily because it:

answers.text: Demonstrated that stars in other galaxies are chemically identical to stars in the Milky Way
Established a reliable method for measuring distances to objects beyond our own galaxy
Provided the first accurate estimate of the age of the universe
