questions.text: What are the three main independent lines of evidence that support the Big Bang model?

answers.text: The expanding universe, Big Bang nucleosynthesis, and the cosmic microwave background
Hubble's Law, the orbit of planets around stars, and the discovery of black holes
The cosmic microwave background, the existence of dark matter, and the structure of galaxies
The redshift of distant galaxies, the discovery of exoplanets, and the age of the Sun

questions.text: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered the cosmic microwave background in 1964. What was the nature of their discovery?

answers.text: They inferred the CMB's existence by calculating the temperature the universe must have been at recombination
They found a faint, uniform microwave signal from all directions that they initially thought was equipment noise
They detected the CMB by measuring the temperature of deep space from a satellite in Earth orbit
They deliberately searched for the predicted CMB signal using a newly built radio telescope

questions.text: Vera Rubin's observations of galaxy rotation curves provided evidence for dark matter because:

answers.text: Stars at the outer edges of galaxies were moving slower than expected, indicating they were being held back by dark matter
Stars at the outer edges of galaxies were rotating faster than expected given the visible mass, implying unseen mass
Galaxies with more dark matter were observed to emit less visible light than galaxies with less dark matter
The rotation of galaxies was found to be opposite in direction to theoretical predictions from general relativity

questions.text: Dark energy was inferred from observations of distant Type Ia supernovae in 1998. What did those observations reveal that was unexpected?

answers.text: The supernovae were dimmer than expected, indicating the universe's expansion is accelerating
The supernovae were brighter than expected, indicating they were closer than their redshift suggested
The supernovae showed no redshift, indicating a static region of the universe at great distances
The supernovae were dimmer than expected, indicating the universe is expanding more slowly than predicted

questions.text: The current best estimate for the composition of the universe by energy content is approximately:

answers.text: 5% ordinary matter, 27% dark matter, 68% dark energy
27% ordinary matter, 5% dark matter, 68% dark energy
50% ordinary matter, 30% dark matter, 20% dark energy
5% ordinary matter, 68% dark matter, 27% dark energy

questions.text: Which of the three proposed fates of the universe do current observations most favor, and why?

answers.text: An oscillating universe, because the CMB shows cyclic temperature patterns consistent with repeated expansions
The Big Freeze, because current observations show accelerating expansion with no sign of reversal
The Big Crunch, because gravity will eventually overcome the expansion as the universe ages
The Big Rip, because dark energy has been directly observed to be strengthening over time

questions.text: The cosmic microwave background was released at the moment called recombination, approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang. What happened at that moment that allowed the CMB to exist?

answers.text: The universe cooled enough for protons and electrons to combine into neutral hydrogen, making the universe transparent to light for the first time
The first stars ignited and their radiation heated the surrounding gas, creating the microwave background
Dark energy first became active, pushing the universe apart and releasing the energy stored in the plasma
Gravity overcame the expansion briefly, compressing matter and releasing a burst of radiation

questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the three main types of galaxies?

answers.text: Disk, spherical, and amorphous
Spiral, elliptical, and irregular
Elliptical, lenticular, and dwarf
Spiral, barred, and ringed

questions.text: Where is our Sun located within the Milky Way galaxy?

answers.text: Approximately 26,000 light-years from the center, in a minor spiral arm
At the outer edge of the galactic disk, beyond the last spiral arm
Equidistant between two major spiral arms, at exactly half the galaxy's radius
At the center of the galactic bulge

questions.text: What is the cosmic web?

answers.text: A theoretical model of parallel universes connected by wormholes
The large-scale structure of the universe consisting of galaxy filaments surrounding vast empty voids
The pattern of gravitational lensing produced by dark matter around galaxy clusters
The network of electromagnetic radiation that connects all stars in the galaxy

questions.text: Which exoplanet detection method works by precisely measuring the dimming of a star's light when a planet passes in front of it?

answers.text: Transit method
Direct imaging
Radial velocity method
Astrometry

questions.text: The habitable zone around a star is defined as the region where:

answers.text: A planet's surface temperature would remain between 0°C and 100°C regardless of atmosphere
A planet could maintain liquid water on its surface given a suitable atmosphere
A planet would be protected from cosmic radiation by the star's magnetic field
A planet would have an oxygen-nitrogen atmosphere similar to Earth's

questions.text: The Fermi paradox refers to:

answers.text: The contradiction between the mathematical likelihood of extraterrestrial civilizations and the absence of any evidence for them
The paradox that light from distant galaxies appears redshifted even though the galaxies are not moving away from us
The fact that despite knowing atomic theory, we cannot observe individual atoms with visible light
The observation that the universe contains far more matter than antimatter

questions.text: What is a biosignature in the context of exoplanet research?

answers.text: The electromagnetic signal produced by technological civilizations on other worlds
A chemical or physical indicator in a planetary atmosphere that is difficult to explain without biological activity
The gravitational signature a planet produces in its star's spectrum
Direct photographic evidence of vegetation on an exoplanet's surface

questions.text: The James Webb Space Telescope detected carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of WASP-39b using which technique?

answers.text: Radial velocity Doppler spectroscopy
Transmission spectroscopy
Direct imaging with adaptive optics
Thermal infrared mapping

questions.text: The "overview effect" reported by many astronauts after seeing Earth from space is best described as:

answers.text: A visual distortion of depth perception caused by the absence of atmospheric perspective in orbit
A cognitive and emotional shift in which Earth appears fragile and borders invisible, producing a heightened sense of planetary unity and responsibility
The disorienting experience of losing gravitational orientation in microgravity during a spacewalk
A telescopic illusion that makes the Moon appear larger than Earth when viewed from the lunar surface

questions.text: The Earthrise photograph, taken by astronaut William Anders during Apollo 8 in December 1968, showed:

answers.text: The full disk of Earth photographed from the lunar surface as the Sun rose behind it
Earth rising above the lunar horizon against the blackness of space, taken from lunar orbit
Earth viewed through a telescope mounted on the Apollo spacecraft during the trans-lunar coast
The first photograph taken on the lunar surface showing Earth in the sky overhead

quizzes.title: Semester 2 Final Exam
quizzes.description: Part 1: 70 multiple-choice questions (1 point each). Part 2: 3 CER short-response items (10 points each). 100 points total. One attempt.

questions.text: A scientist finds a fossil of a fish-like creature with fin-limb structures and a neck, dated to the Devonian period (~375 million years ago). This fossil would best be described as which of the following?

answers.text: A transitional fossil showing features of two major animal groups
A vestigial structure
A homologous structure
Evidence of convergent evolution

questions.text: Darwin observed that the finch species on the Galapagos Islands are most closely related to a finch species from the South American mainland, rather than to finch species from other islands with similar climates. This observation best supports which conclusion?

answers.text: Galapagos finches evolved independently from all South American birds
The Galapagos finches descended from South American ancestors that colonized the islands and then diversified
Galapagos finches were placed on the islands by a common design process
Climate is the primary factor determining which species exist in a given location

questions.text: A population of moths varies in wing color. This variation is heritable. Dark-colored moths are more visible to predators in a pale-bark forest and reproduce less than pale-colored moths. The population is large. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

answers.text: Natural selection cannot occur because the moths do not choose their wing color
Natural selection will occur, but only if the moths intentionally change their wing color in response to predators
Natural selection will occur because all four required conditions are present
Natural selection will not occur because the population is too large for selection to matter

questions.text: In a population of fish, individuals with medium body size survive better than very small or very large individuals, because medium fish are better able to avoid both predators (who prefer smaller fish) and competition from larger fish of other species. Over many generations, the average body size remains stable. This is an example of which type of natural selection?

answers.text: Directional selection
Disruptive selection
Artificial selection
Stabilizing selection

questions.text: Genetic drift has a greater effect on allele frequencies in small populations than in large populations because:

answers.text: Random sampling error is larger relative to the population size, so chance events can dramatically shift allele frequencies
Small populations mutate faster, producing more new alleles
Small populations receive more gene flow from neighboring populations
Natural selection is weaker in small populations, allowing drift to operate more freely

questions.text: Which of the following correctly distinguishes intrasexual selection from intersexual selection?

answers.text: Intrasexual selection involves mate choice by one sex; intersexual selection involves competition between individuals of the same sex
Intrasexual selection involves competition between individuals of the same sex; intersexual selection involves mate choice exercised by one sex
Intrasexual selection occurs in plants; intersexual selection occurs only in animals
Intrasexual selection favors survival traits; intersexual selection favors mating traits

questions.text: A population geneticist finds that the observed genotype frequencies in a population differ significantly from the Hardy-Weinberg predictions. The best interpretation of this finding is:

answers.text: The Hardy-Weinberg principle has been disproved for this population
The population is not evolving and all five conditions are being met
One or more of the five Hardy-Weinberg conditions is being violated, and an evolutionary force is operating at this locus
The calculations must contain an error, because real populations always match Hardy-Weinberg predictions

questions.text: The Permian-Triassic extinction, approximately 252 million years ago, is notable for which reason?

answers.text: It was caused by an asteroid impact, the same mechanism responsible for the K-Pg extinction.
It eliminated the non-avian dinosaurs and cleared the ecological stage for the mammalian adaptive radiation.
It occurred at the boundary between the Cretaceous and Paleogene periods and is preserved in a globally distributed iridium layer.
It is estimated to have eliminated 90 to 96 percent of all marine species, making it the largest mass extinction in Earth's history.

questions.text: In the binomial nomenclature system, which of the following is written correctly?

answers.text: *Homo sapiens*
homo sapiens
*Homo Sapiens*
homo Sapiens

questions.text: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between Bacteria and Archaea?

answers.text: Bacteria and Archaea are both prokaryotes and are therefore more closely related to each other than either is to eukaryotes.
Bacteria and Archaea both lack a membrane-bound nucleus, but they are not closely related; Archaea are more closely related to eukaryotes than to bacteria.
Archaea are a subgroup of bacteria that evolved adaptations for extreme environments, which explains their unusual biochemistry.
Bacteria and Archaea form a single domain together, which is then divided into eukaryotes, making three total domains of life.

questions.text: A clade is correctly defined as which of the following?

answers.text: A group of organisms that share the same ecological niche and compete for the same resources.
A group of organisms that are morphologically similar, regardless of their evolutionary relationships.
An ancestral species and all of its descendants — a complete branch of the evolutionary tree.
The set of shared derived characters used to identify a particular taxonomic group in a cladistic analysis.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes why Protista is considered a paraphyletic group rather than a true clade (monophyletic group)?

answers.text: Protista contains too many species from too many different environments to form a single clade.
Protista includes organisms from multiple completely separate evolutionary lineages with no common ancestor.
Protista was defined before DNA evidence was available, so it groups organisms that have since been shown to be completely unrelated.
Protista includes a common ancestor but excludes some of that ancestor's descendants, specifically the animals, plants, and fungi that evolved from within protist lineages.

questions.text: The hominin fossil record shows that bipedalism (upright walking on two legs) evolved:

answers.text: Before the dramatic expansion of brain size, with species like Australopithecus already fully bipedal while retaining a brain the size of a chimpanzee's.
At approximately the same time as the dramatic expansion of brain size in the hominin lineage.
After the dramatic expansion of brain size, supporting the view that increased intelligence enabled the evolution of upright walking.
Only in the genus Homo, after bipedalism and brain expansion evolved together as a linked package.

questions.text: The Miller-Urey experiment (1953) demonstrated that:

answers.text: The complete pathway from simple chemistry to the first living cell can be replicated in a laboratory setting.
Amino acids and other organic molecules, the building blocks of life, can form spontaneously from simple inorganic molecules under simulated early-Earth conditions.
Life must have originated in the deep ocean at hydrothermal vents rather than in surface water, as originally assumed.
RNA was the first self-replicating molecule on early Earth, supporting the RNA world hypothesis.

questions.text: The ecological niche of an organism is best described as:

answers.text: The physical location where an organism lives, including the specific microhabitat it prefers within a larger ecosystem.
The geographic range across which a species can be found, including all the biomes and climate zones it can tolerate.
The full functional role of an organism in its ecosystem, including what it eats, when it is active, how it uses space, and what role it plays in nutrient cycling.
The set of environmental conditions (temperature range, rainfall, soil type) within which an organism can survive and reproduce.

questions.text: The 10 percent rule in ecology states that:

answers.text: Approximately 10 percent of all species in an ecosystem are producers; the remaining 90 percent are consumers or decomposers.
A population can sustain a harvest of up to 10 percent of its individuals per year without declining below its carrying capacity.
Decomposers return approximately 10 percent of nutrients from dead organic matter back to the soil each year; the rest is permanently stored in sediment.
Only approximately 10 percent of the energy available at one trophic level is transferred to the next trophic level; the remaining 90 percent is lost as heat or used for metabolic processes.

questions.text: Why is atmospheric nitrogen (N2) unavailable to most organisms even though the atmosphere is 78 percent nitrogen?

answers.text: The triple bond holding the two nitrogen atoms together in N2 is extremely strong, and most organisms lack the enzymes needed to break it and convert N2 into usable forms such as ammonium or nitrate.
Atmospheric nitrogen is in a gaseous state and must be dissolved in water before organisms can absorb it; only aquatic organisms can access nitrogen directly from solution.
Atmospheric nitrogen exists only in the upper atmosphere and does not diffuse down to the surface in concentrations high enough for biological uptake.
Nitrogen gas is toxic to most organisms at high concentrations and cannot be absorbed directly without causing cellular damage.

questions.text: A population exhibiting logistic growth will:

answers.text: Continue to grow at an accelerating rate indefinitely as long as immigration rates remain higher than emigration rates in the population.
Grow rapidly when well below carrying capacity, then slow as it approaches carrying capacity, eventually leveling off at or near K.
Grow exponentially until a sudden collapse, after which the population crashes to near zero before recovering and repeating the cycle.
Grow at a constant linear rate determined by the birth rate minus the death rate, regardless of current population size or resource availability.

questions.text: Interspecific competition is classified using the plus/minus/zero framework as:

answers.text: Plus/plus, because both species gain access to the shared resource
Plus/zero, because one species benefits and the other is unaffected
Minus/minus, because both species are harmed by reduced access to the shared resource
Plus/minus, because one species outcompetes the other and gains the resource entirely

questions.text: What is the key difference between primary succession and secondary succession?

answers.text: Primary succession occurs in forested areas; secondary succession occurs in aquatic ecosystems
Primary succession is driven by facilitation; secondary succession is driven by competition alone
Primary succession leads to a climax community; secondary succession loops back to bare substrate repeatedly
Primary succession occurs on bare substrate with no prior soil or biological community; secondary succession occurs in areas where the soil remains intact from a previous community

questions.text: Robert Paine's field experiment on the Washington coast demonstrated which concept by removing sea stars from an intertidal community?

answers.text: The keystone species concept, showing that a species can have an ecological impact far greater than its abundance or biomass would predict
Competitive exclusion, showing that two species cannot share the same ecological niche
The intermediate disturbance hypothesis, showing that moderate predation levels maintain biodiversity
Resource partitioning, showing that coexisting species use different microhabitats within the same community

questions.text: Which two environmental variables most directly determine which biome is found in a given location?

answers.text: Soil type and elevation
Temperature and annual precipitation
Sunlight hours and wind speed
Latitude and longitude

questions.text: The photic zone in an aquatic ecosystem is defined as the region where:

answers.text: Temperature remains constant year-round
Dissolved oxygen is lowest
Enough sunlight penetrates to support photosynthesis
Decomposer organisms are most abundant

questions.text: Species evenness refers to:

answers.text: The total number of different species in a community
The geographic range of a species across multiple biomes
The similarity in species composition between two nearby communities
How uniformly individual organisms are distributed across species in a community

questions.text: The equilibrium theory of island biogeography (MacArthur and Wilson) predicts that a small island far from the mainland will have:

answers.text: Low immigration rate and high extinction rate, producing low species richness
High immigration rate and low extinction rate, producing high species richness
Low immigration rate and low extinction rate, producing moderate species richness
High immigration rate and high extinction rate, producing moderate species richness

questions.text: Eutrophication in aquatic ecosystems causes fish kills primarily because:

answers.text: Excess algae directly consume all the oxygen in the water
Decomposition of dead algal biomass by bacteria depletes dissolved oxygen, creating hypoxic conditions
Fertilizer compounds are directly toxic to fish at high concentrations
Algal blooms block sunlight that fish need to navigate and find food

questions.text: Biomagnification refers to:

answers.text: The increase in the size of organisms at higher trophic levels
The process by which toxic chemicals are diluted as they move up the food chain
The amplification of pollutant concentration at each successive trophic level, as predators accumulate the pollutant from all their prey
The increase in primary productivity caused by nutrient addition to an ecosystem

questions.text: The Kissimmee River restoration project succeeded primarily because:

answers.text: Ecologists transplanted millions of native plant and animal species back into the degraded river sections
Invasive species in the channelized canal were removed by chemical treatment before the restoration began
The Army Corps of Engineers rebuilt the original floodplain wetlands by importing native soil from other Florida sites
Restoring the river's natural meandering channel and seasonal flooding allowed the biological community to recover through natural recolonization

questions.text: The asthenosphere is significant because it:

answers.text: Is the zone of partially plastic rock on which the rigid lithospheric plates move
Is the layer where Earth's magnetic field is generated by liquid iron-nickel
Is the outermost solid layer of Earth, composed of granite and basalt
Is the boundary between the outer core and the inner core

questions.text: Paleomagnetic stripes are symmetric on both sides of a mid-ocean ridge because:

answers.text: Earth's magnetic field alternates direction precisely every time a new section of ocean floor is created at the ridge
New oceanic crust is created at the ridge and spreads equally in both directions, with each section recording the magnetic field polarity at the time it solidified
The ridge itself acts as a barrier that reverses the magnetic field on one side relative to the other
Symmetric stripes are a mathematical artifact of how magnetometers measure ocean floor magnetism

questions.text: Which of the following is the most direct evidence that seafloor spreading is occurring today, not just in the geological past?

answers.text: The symmetric pattern of paleomagnetic stripes on both sides of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge
Matching fossils of the freshwater reptile Mesosaurus on both South America and Africa
GPS stations in North America and Europe moving apart at rates consistent with seafloor spreading predictions
The alignment of the Appalachian Mountains with mountain ranges in Scotland and Scandinavia

questions.text: A geologist examines two samples of igneous rock. Sample A has large, easily visible crystals; Sample B is fine-grained with crystals too small to see without a magnifying lens. What does the crystal size difference indicate about each sample's formation history?

answers.text: Sample A formed at Earth's surface from lava; Sample B formed deep underground from magma.
Sample A is metamorphic; Sample B is igneous. Crystal size differences distinguish rock type, not formation speed.
Sample A formed from magma with more minerals; Sample B formed from magma with fewer minerals, producing smaller crystals.
Sample A formed slowly deep underground from magma; Sample B formed rapidly at the surface from lava.

questions.text: Which of the following rock types most commonly displays foliation, and what produces this texture?

answers.text: Metamorphic rock; foliation forms when directed pressure causes flat minerals (especially mica) to align in parallel layers.
Igneous rock; foliation forms when magma cools slowly and minerals align in the direction of heat flow.
Sedimentary rock; foliation forms when layers of sediment are compressed horizontally during lithification.
Igneous rock; foliation forms when lava flows in sheets across the surface and the layers solidify one at a time.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly explains why S-waves (secondary seismic waves) do not travel through Earth's outer core?

answers.text: The outer core is too hot for S-waves to propagate; heat destroys shear wave motion in solid rock.
S-waves require solid material to transmit shear motion; the outer core is liquid, and liquids cannot resist shear, so S-waves stop at the core boundary.
S-waves are too slow to penetrate the dense iron-nickel core and are absorbed by the core material before passing through.
S-waves are blocked by the extreme pressure at the core boundary, which reflects them back toward the surface.

questions.text: James Hutton proposed uniformitarianism in the late 1700s. Which of the following best describes what uniformitarianism claims?

answers.text: Earth is approximately 6,000 years old, and its geological features were formed rapidly by a series of catastrophic floods.
Earth's geological history is divided into separate intervals defined by sudden, dramatic changes that are fundamentally different from any process operating today.

The geological processes acting on Earth today (erosion, deposition, volcanic activity) are the same kinds of processes that shaped Earth in the past, and they have operated over an immense span of time.
Geological features form at unpredictable rates that vary by location, making it impossible to compare rock layers from different regions.

questions.text: A geologist examining a cliff face sees three horizontal sedimentary rock layers (oldest at the bottom, youngest at the top) cut through by a diagonal vein of granite. Using the principle of cross-cutting relationships, what can she conclude about the granite?

answers.text: The granite formed before the sedimentary layers, because granite is a harder rock and must have formed first.
The granite formed at the same time as the middle sedimentary layer, because it is found in contact with all three layers.
The granite formed after the top layer only, because the cross-cutting relationship applies only to the youngest layer the intrusion contacts.
The granite formed after all three sedimentary layers, because an intrusion can only cut through rock that already exists.

questions.text: A geologist is searching for an index fossil to correlate rock layers across two different continents. Which combination of characteristics would make an organism the best candidate for an index fossil?

answers.text: Short-lived species (existed for a brief geological interval) that was geographically widespread and abundant, leaving distinctive, easily identified remains.
Long-lived species with a small geographic range and hard shells that preserve well in sediment.
Long-lived species with a wide geographic range, because its presence across many locations confirms its reliability as a marker.
Short-lived species confined to deep-water marine environments, because deep-water sediments are better preserved and less disturbed by erosion.

questions.text: What defines the boundaries between intervals (eons, eras, periods) on the geologic time scale?

answers.text: Equal divisions of elapsed time -- each interval represents the same number of millions of years.
Major transitions in the fossil record, most commonly mass extinctions followed by the rapid diversification of new life forms in the subsequent layers.
Changes in rock type -- each new interval begins when the dominant rock type changes from sedimentary to igneous or vice versa.
Geographic boundaries -- each interval is defined by the position of the continents at that time in Earth's history.

questions.text: A spacecraft traveling at 15,000 m/s in deep space turns off its engines. There is no air resistance and no significant gravitational pull from any nearby body. What does Newton's First Law predict will happen to the spacecraft's velocity?

answers.text: It gradually slows to a stop over several hours, because motion naturally decreases without an engine to maintain it.
It speeds up, because removing the engine's backward exhaust thrust allows the spacecraft to accelerate freely.
It continues at 15,000 m/s in a straight line indefinitely, because the net force on it is zero.
It slows momentarily, then returns to 15,000 m/s, because the spacecraft seeks its "natural" equilibrium speed.

questions.text: A net force of 15 N acts on a 3 kg object. What is the object's acceleration?

answers.text: 45 m/s², because acceleration equals force multiplied by mass.
0.2 m/s², because acceleration equals mass divided by force.
12 m/s², because acceleration equals force minus mass.
5 m/s², because a = F/m = 15 N / 3 kg = 5 m/s².

questions.text: Newton's Third Law states that for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. A student argues that this means all forces in the universe cancel out and nothing can ever accelerate. What is wrong with this reasoning?

answers.text: The student is wrong because action and reaction forces act on different objects and therefore cannot cancel each other. Forces cancel only when they act on the same object.
The student is correct; Newton's Third Law does mean all forces cancel, but objects can still accelerate because of velocity already stored in them.
The student is wrong because action and reaction forces are not always exactly equal -- they are only approximately equal for small objects.
The student is wrong because the Third Law only applies to contact forces, not to gravity or other field forces.

questions.text: A book rests on a table. Earth pulls the book downward with a gravitational force of 20 N. According to Newton's Third Law, what is the reaction to this gravitational force?

answers.text: The table pushes the book upward with a normal force of 20 N.
The book pulls Earth upward with a gravitational force of 20 N.
The book pushes down on the table with a contact force of 20 N.
Gravity pulls the table downward with a force of 20 N.

questions.text: According to Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation, if the distance between two objects is doubled while their masses remain the same, the gravitational force between them becomes:

answers.text: Twice as large, because force is proportional to distance.
One-half as large, because force is inversely proportional to the distance.
One-quarter as large, because force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
Unchanged, because the masses have not changed.

questions.text: A 60 kg astronaut on Earth weighs approximately 588 N. The same astronaut travels to a planet where the gravitational field strength is 3.7 m/s². Which statement is correct about the astronaut's mass and weight on that planet?

answers.text: Both the mass and the weight remain 60 kg and 588 N, because the astronaut's body has not changed.
Both the mass and the weight decrease proportionally, because a weaker gravitational field reduces the amount of matter an object contains in that environment.
The weight remains 588 N, but the mass decreases, because mass is determined by the gravitational field and would be lower in a weaker field.
The mass remains 60 kg, but the weight decreases to 60 × 3.7 = 222 N, because weight depends on the local gravitational field strength.

questions.text: An object moves at constant speed in a circle. In which direction does its centripetal acceleration point?

answers.text: Toward the center of the circle, perpendicular to the velocity at every point.
In the same direction as the object's velocity, tangent to the circular path.
Away from the center of the circle, in the direction of the apparent centrifugal force.
Straight down, because gravity provides the centripetal acceleration in all circular motion.

questions.text: Kepler's Second Law states that a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals. Which of the following correctly describes what this means for a planet's orbital speed?

answers.text: The planet moves at constant speed throughout its orbit, because equal areas in equal times requires uniform motion.
The planet moves faster when closer to the Sun (near perihelion) and slower when farther from the Sun (near aphelion).
The planet moves faster when farther from the Sun and slower when closer, to compensate for the larger orbital radius.
The planet moves at the same average speed regardless of its distance from the Sun, since the total area swept per year is fixed.

questions.text: A person carries a briefcase horizontally at constant height from one end of a hallway to the other. Which of the following correctly describes the work done by gravity on the briefcase during this trip?

answers.text: Gravity does positive work equal to mgh, where h is the height the briefcase is carried above the floor.
Gravity does negative work equal to −mgd, where d is the horizontal distance traveled, because gravity opposes the horizontal motion.
Gravity does zero work on the briefcase because the gravitational force acts downward while the displacement is horizontal; the angle between force and displacement is 90 degrees, making cos 90° = 0.
Gravity does work equal to mgd because gravity is always acting on the briefcase and the briefcase moves a distance d.

questions.text: A car increases its speed from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. By what factor does its kinetic energy increase?

answers.text: The kinetic energy increases by a factor of 2, because doubling the speed doubles the kinetic energy.
The kinetic energy increases by a factor of 8, because kinetic energy depends on v³ for high-speed objects.
The kinetic energy increases by a factor of 1, because kinetic energy depends on mass and the mass does not change.
The kinetic energy increases by a factor of 4, because kinetic energy depends on v² and (20)²/(10)² = 400/100 = 4.

questions.text: A frictionless pendulum is released from rest at a height h above its lowest point. At the lowest point of its swing, which statement correctly describes the energy state of the pendulum?

answers.text: All of the pendulum's initial gravitational potential energy has converted to kinetic energy; KE at the bottom equals mgh.
The pendulum has zero total mechanical energy because it started from rest, and rest implies no energy.
The kinetic energy at the bottom is equal to half the initial potential energy; the other half has been lost to the environment.
The pendulum's kinetic energy at the bottom equals its potential energy at the top minus its weight times the height.

questions.text: A machine has an input energy of 500 J and produces 350 J of useful work output. What is its efficiency, and what happens to the remaining energy?

answers.text: Efficiency = 70%; the remaining 150 J is destroyed by friction and no longer exists as energy.
Efficiency = 70%; the remaining 150 J is converted to thermal energy (heat) through friction and other non-conservative forces, warming the machine and its surroundings.
Efficiency = 150%; the machine adds 150 J more than it uses because friction helps rather than hinders energy output.
Efficiency = 70%; the remaining 30% is stored as potential energy inside the machine, available for future use.

questions.text: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been sitting at room temperature (22°C) for several hours. When you pick up each one, the metal spoon feels noticeably colder. What is the correct explanation?

answers.text: The metal spoon has a lower temperature than the wooden spoon because metal absorbs more cold from the room air.
The metal spoon has a lower temperature because its shiny surface reflects heat and prevents it from warming fully.
Both spoons are at 22°C, but the metal conducts heat away from your hand much faster than wood, causing your hand to lose heat rapidly and creating the sensation of cold.
Both spoons are at 22°C, but wood contains more stored thermal energy per gram, so it transfers more heat to your hand and feels warmer.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly states what the Second Law of Thermodynamics says about the entropy of an isolated system?

answers.text: Entropy decreases as the system reaches thermal equilibrium.
Entropy remains exactly constant in all real physical processes.
Entropy may increase or decrease depending on whether the process is exothermic or endothermic.
Entropy always increases or remains constant; it never spontaneously decreases in an isolated system.

questions.text: A heat engine operates between a hot reservoir at 500 K and a cold reservoir at 250 K. Using the Carnot efficiency formula, what is the maximum possible efficiency of this engine?

answers.text: 50%, calculated as 1 − Tᴄ/Tₕ = 1 − 250/500 = 0.50.
100%, because the temperature ratio Tₕ/Tᴄ = 500/250 = 2.0, and the engine can theoretically convert twice the cold reservoir temperature into work.
25%, because real engines always achieve one-half the Carnot limit, and the theoretical Carnot efficiency here is 50%.

questions.text: A sound wave in air has a frequency of 256 Hz and a wavelength of 1.34 m. What is the wave speed?

answers.text: 257 m/s. Add frequency and wavelength: 256 + 1.34 ≈ 257.

questions.text: A train moving toward a stationary observer sounds its horn. Compared to the actual frequency the horn emits, what frequency does the observer hear?

answers.text: A lower frequency, because the horn's sound energy must overcome the distance the train is traveling.
The same frequency, because the speed of sound in air is independent of the speed of the source.
A higher frequency, because the train's motion compresses the wavefronts ahead of it, shortening the wavelength and increasing the frequency detected by the observer.
A lower frequency, because the train is moving away from the horn's sound waves, stretching them out.

questions.text: A scientist heats a sample of pure sodium gas and observes the light it emits through a diffraction grating. She sees two bright yellow lines on an otherwise dark background at specific wavelengths. What do these bright yellow lines represent?

answers.text: All the wavelengths of visible light that sodium reflects; the dark regions are the wavelengths it absorbs.
Background radiation from the Sun that sodium atoms scatter in the yellow portion of the spectrum.
The emission spectrum of the heating element, which always produces yellow light at high temperatures.
